section_summary: This section documents Japanese censorship of American books, magazines, and newspapers between 1936 and 1939, including exclusions for alleged lèse-majesté, indecency, criticism of the Japanese Army, and threats to public order. It also covers American efforts to have prohibited books returned rather than confiscated and a police ban on reporting military measures in Japan’s southwestern territories and northern Korea. The final documents concern suppression of Yukio Ozaki’s argument that Japan should remain neutral in a future European war.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 162 on the Suppression of Current History’s May Issue
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports the stated reason for suppression in Japan of the May issue of Current History.
subfiles.summary: Telegram 162: Current History's selling agent was told the May issue was suppressed over Charles Hodges's article 'Japanese Enigma'.

subfiles.title: Letter to Current History Explaining the Suppression of Its May Issue
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Relays the American Embassy’s information concerning the suppression of Current History in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Department tells Current History its selling agent learned the May issue was suppressed for Hodges's 'Japanese Enigma'.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment from Current History
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the Department’s correspondence concerning suppression of the magazine’s May issue.
subfiles.summary: Current History thanks the Department for its July 29 and 30 letters on the May issue's suppression.

subfiles.title: Disposition of American Books Excluded from Japan
subfiles.from: E. R. Dickover, Chargé d’Affaires ad interim
subfiles.about: Reports an effort to secure the return, rather than confiscation, of American books denied entry into Japan.
subfiles.summary: Dickover forwards W. S. Hall's request that excluded American books be returned to senders rather than confiscated; the Embassy gave the Foreign Office an informal memorandum and the American Affairs bureau chief promised investigation.

subfiles.title: Letter from W. S. Hall on Confiscation of Imported Books
subfiles.about: Protests the confiscation of foreign books and asks that prohibited titles instead be returned to their senders.
subfiles.summary: Hall accepts Japan's right to ban books but objects to confiscation, which harms Japanese booksellers and discourages orders, urging return of banned books; his firms sell no erotica.

subfiles.title: Informal Memorandum on Returning Excluded American Books
subfiles.to: Chief, Bureau of American Affairs, Japanese Foreign Office
subfiles.about: Requests a change in Japanese practice so that excluded American books may be returned instead of confiscated.
subfiles.summary: Memo: uncertainty about which books will be banned deters Japanese buyers; returning excluded books would still protect Japan without hurting American publishers.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on the Ban of Fortune
subfiles.about: Records an understanding of why Fortune magazine was banned.
subfiles.summary: Note: Fortune was banned because it discussed matters under press censorship; no further detail.

subfiles.title: American Books and Magazines Recently Excluded from Japan
subfiles.from: E. R. Dickover, Chargé d’Affaires ad interim
subfiles.about: Lists foreign books and periodicals recently denied entry into Japan and their reported grounds for exclusion.
subfiles.summary: Dickover reports exclusion of September 1936 Fortune and Literary Digest for lèse-majesté, Film Fun for indecency, and Yakhontov's Eyes on Japan; Stimson's The Far Eastern Crisis was admitted after Foreign Office opposition to a ban.

subfiles.title: Press Ban on Certain Military Measures
subfiles.about: Reports police instructions restricting publication of information about military measures in several Japanese-controlled regions.
subfiles.summary: On February 4 newspapers were told to publish only official statements on military measures in the southwestern islands, Taiwan, Ogasawara or northern Korea; the Embassy does not know whether to conceal operations or prevent rumors.

subfiles.title: Internal Note on Confiscation of American Periodicals
subfiles.about: Summarizes the reported reasons for confiscating American periodicals in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Note: the Embassy reported confiscation of American periodicals for perceived disrespect to the Emperor and criticism of the Army.

subfiles.title: American Magazines Recently Excluded
subfiles.about: Reports the confiscation of the March Living Age and April Esquire in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Grew: the March Living Age was confiscated for a remark deemed disrespectful to the Emperor, and April Esquire for a caricature of a Japanese general as 'Lawrence of Japan' and criticism of Army China policy.

subfiles.title: Duplicate Copy of “American Magazines Recently Excluded”
subfiles.about: Duplicates the report on Japanese confiscation of Living Age and Esquire.
subfiles.summary: This degraded duplicate repeats the report that Living Age was confiscated for disrespect toward the Emperor. It also repeats that Esquire was suppressed because of a caricature comparing a Japanese general to Lawrence and criticism of Japanese Army policy in China.

subfiles.title: Internal Note on Suppression of the Japan Advertiser
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs; Ballantine
subfiles.about: Summarizes the suppression of the July 4 Japan Advertiser over an article by Yukio Ozaki advocating neutrality.
subfiles.summary: Note: the Japan Advertiser was suppressed for Ozaki's argument that Japan stay neutral, perhaps because he said Germany and Italy offered no compensation for joining them.

subfiles.title: Suppression of Japan Advertiser of July 4, 1939
subfiles.from: Eugene H. Dooman, Chargé d’Affaires ad interim
subfiles.about: Reports and explains police suppression of a Japan Advertiser issue containing Yukio Ozaki’s neutrality article.
subfiles.summary: Dooman: the Japan Advertiser of July 4, 1939 was suppressed under a public-order provision for Ozaki's frank discussion of Germany and Italy; remaining copies were confiscated; Nippon Hyoron and Contemporary Opinions were also suppressed.

subfiles.title: Riches, Power Seen for Japan if Neutral in Next World War
subfiles.doc_type: newspaper clipping; enclosure to despatch No. 4014
subfiles.about: Argues that Japan should remain neutral in a future European war to avoid destruction and gain wealth and international power.
subfiles.summary: Ozaki says neutrality in the next war would bring wealth like the First World War, rejects aligning with Germany and Italy, cites Arita's limited reading of the Anti-Comintern Pact, and says neutrality could leave Japan and the US the strongest powers.
